n: This verse completes the woes of chapter 9: woe to lawmakers who write unjust laws and officials who issue oppressive rulings.
Their laws deny justice to the needy, rob the poor of their rights, and make widows and orphans their prey. God watches over the vulnerable.

f.w: turn aside the needy from judgment

n: What will they do when God comes to judge and disaster arrives from afar? Where will they run and where will they hide their riches?

f.g: The day God comes to judge.

n: Without God, they will crouch among prisoners or fall among the dead. And still His hand is stretched out — the fourth and final time this refrain appears.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: Now God addresses Assyria as His “rod” — a tool He uses to discipline His people. 2 Nephi 20:5 reads “their indignation.”

f.g: The empire based in northern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), dominant from about 745 to 612 BC.

n: God sends Assyria against godless Israel to plunder it and trample it like mud in the streets.
But Assyria doesn’t know it is God’s tool. Its king only wants to conquer and destroy as many nations as possible.
The Assyrian king boasts that even his commanders are as great as kings. Assyrian rulers called themselves “king of kings.”
He lists cities he has conquered — Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Damascus, Samaria — all fell to Assyria in the 700s BC. Jerusalem, he thinks, will be next.

f.g: A major city on the Euphrates, taken by Assyria in 717 BC.
A Syrian city on the Orontes River, conquered 738 and 720 BC.

n: He reasons that he has defeated kingdoms with even more impressive idols than Jerusalem’s or Samaria’s. 2 Nephi 20:10 reads “hath founded.”
Since he destroyed Samaria and its idols, he’s sure he can do the same to Jerusalem. He thinks the Lord is just another idol.

f.w: as I have done unto Samaria

n: But once the Lord finishes using Assyria to discipline Jerusalem, He will punish the proud Assyrian king for his arrogance.
The king boasts that his own strength and cleverness did it all. He erased borders, stole treasures, and toppled kings.

f.w: By the strength of my hand

f.g: Erased national borders — Assyria deported whole populations.

n: He bragged that he gathered the nations’ wealth as easily as a boy collecting eggs from an abandoned nest — no one even flapped a wing or chirped.
Can an axe brag against the person who swings it? Assyria is only a tool in God’s hand, yet acts as if it were in charge.
So the Lord will send a wasting disease among Assyria’s strong warriors and kindle a fire under its glory.
Israel’s Light — the Lord — will become a fire, and the Holy One a flame, burning Assyria’s army like thorns and briers in a single day. This was fulfilled when 185,000 Assyrians died in one night.
The splendor of Assyria’s “forest” and “fields” — its armies and power — will be wiped out completely, like a sick man wasting away.

f.g: Possibly “as when a sick man wastes away.”

n: So few “trees” will be left that a child could count and write them down.
In that day the surviving remnant of Israel will no longer lean on Assyria, who struck them, but will lean truly on the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.
A remnant will return to the mighty God. This echoes the name of Isaiah’s son Shear-jashub and the title “mighty God” in 9:6.
Though Israel be as many as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. The destruction is decreed, but it will overflow with righteousness — justice and redemption together.

f.w: as the sand of the sea

n: The Lord has decided to bring this destruction across the land.
Therefore God tells His people in Zion not to fear Assyria. It will strike them, as Egypt once oppressed Israel, but not forever.

f.w: be not afraid of the Assyrian

n: In a very short while God’s anger toward His people will end and turn against their destroyers.
The Lord will lash Assyria as He did Midian at the rock of Oreb, and raise His rod over the sea as He did at the Red Sea for Moses.

f.w: his rod was upon the sea

n: In that day Assyria’s burden will fall from their shoulders and its yoke from their necks. The yoke will break “because of the anointing” — Latter-day Saints and others see a hint of the Anointed One, the Messiah.

f.g: Hebrew obscure — possibly “because of fatness” (the ox grows too strong for the yoke) or “because of the oil.”

f.w: his yoke from off thy neck

n: Isaiah pictures an army marching south toward Jerusalem through towns just north of the city — Aiath, Migron, Michmash — where it stores its baggage.

f.g: Ai, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem.

n: They cross the ravine pass and camp at Geba. Nearby Ramah trembles and Gibeah, Saul’s hometown, flees. 2 Nephi 20:29 spells it “Ramath.”
The villages cry out in alarm — Gallim, Laish, and poor Anathoth, later Jeremiah’s hometown.
Madmenah’s people flee and Gebim’s residents run for safety.
The invader halts at Nob, within sight of Jerusalem, and shakes his fist at Mount Zion. But that is as far as he gets.

f.g: A town on a hill overlooking Jerusalem (1 Samuel 21:1).

n: Then the Lord, like a forester, will lop off the branches with terrifying power and cut down the tallest trees — the proud Assyrian leaders.

He will chop down the thickets with an axe, and mighty Lebanon — Assyria’s forest-like army — will fall to the Mighty One. Chapter 11 then contrasts this with a new shoot sprouting from Jesse’s stump.
